system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 11 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2168-03-11 22:12:00 to 2168-03-22 20:01:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  Evaluate PICC line placement.

COMPARISON:  ___.

PORTABLE CHEST RADIOGRAPH:  Right-sided PICC is seen with tip at the distal
SVC.  Cardiac and mediastinal contours appear unremarkable.  Lungs appear
clear.

IMPRESSION:  Right-sided PICC with tip overlying the distal SVC.

INDICATION:  Chronic pancreatitis with recurrent abdominal pain.

COMPARISON:  MRCP ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Multiplanar T1- and T2-weighted images of the abdomen were
acquired on a 1.5 Tesla magnet including dynamic 3D imaging obtained prior to,
during, and after the uneventful intravenous administration of 0.1 mmol/kg of
gadolinium-DTPA.  Multiplanar 2D and 3D reformations along with subtraction
images were generated on independent workstation.

MRI OF THE ABDOMEN WITH AND WITHOUT INTRAVENOUS CONTRAST (MRCP):  Main
pancreatic duct demonstrates mild diffuse irregularity but is otherwise normal
in caliber without evidence of focal stenosis or dilatation.  Several small
dilated side branches are identified within the pancreatic neck and tail
measuring up to 4 mm wide.  The pancreatic parenchyma demonstrates mild
diffuse atrophy, but no focal masses are present.  No peripancreatic fluid
collections are demonstrated.  The pancreas enhances homogeneously post-
contrast administration.  No evidence for pancreas divisum.

Again demonstrated within segment VI of the liver is an 8-mm hemangioma,
unchanged.  A second, 5-mm well-circumscribed round lesion which is
homogeneously hypointense with respect to the liver parenchyma on T1-weighted
images and hyperintense on T2- weighted imaging is located within segment ___,
immediately anterior to the inferior vena cava. This lesion enhances, becoming
isointense with respect to the hepatic parenchyma on all post-contrast phases
of imaging and also likely represents another hemangioma, unchanged.  No new
focal masses are otherwise demonstrated.  No intra- or extra-hepatic biliary
duct dilatation is identified.  Hepatic arteries, hepatic veins, and portal
veins are widely patent.

The gallbladder is absent. The spleen, adrenal glands, left kidney, visualized
bowel loops are within normal limits.  7mm simple cyst is seen in the upper
pole of the right kidney. No hydronephrosis or new renal masses.  Abdominal
aorta is normal in caliber. No free fluid.  No pathologically enlarged
mesenteric or retroperitoneal lymph nodes.

No suspicious focal bone marrow signal abnormalities are identified.

Multiplanar 2D and 3D reformations were essential in providing multiple
perspectives for the dynamic series.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Mild irregularity of the main pancreatic duct with a few tiny dilated side
branches, findings compatible with prior pancreatitis.  No pancreatic duct
strictures or pseudocysts present.
2.  Two hemangiomas within the liver, unchanged.
3.  Simple right renal cyst.

AP CHEST 12:09 A.M ___  

HISTORY:  Pancreatitis.  PICC line.

IMPRESSION:  AP chest compared to ___:

Right PICC line has been removed.  New left PICC line ends at the superior
cavoatrial junction.  Lungs are clear.  There is no pleural abnormality,
evidence of central adenopathy or mediastinal widening.  Heart size is normal.
Pager ___ was paged as requested.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. I’ve been having this sharp pain in my upper right abdomen again. It’s been getting worse with eating, drinking, even just moving around.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds familiar. You’ve had pancreatitis before, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, several times. Last time was a few months ago. I was in the hospital for five days, felt better for a day, then the pain came back full force.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That’s consistent with recurrent pancreatitis. We’ll keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now to let your pancreas rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I’m really thirsty. Can I have ice chips?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can give you ice chips for now. You’ll get fluids through your IV to stay hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. The pain is pretty bad. Is there anything you can give me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re starting you on hydromorphone through a PCA pump so you can control your pain safely. We’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m just worried this will never get better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But you’ve improved before, and we’ll work to get you through this flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night show low white blood cells and mild anemia, but nothing too alarming.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Low white blood cells? Does that mean I’m more at risk for infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can, but we’re watching closely. It’s common during pancreatitis flares. We’ll keep an eye on your temperature and symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about the PICC line I saw the nurse placing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a PICC line in your right arm so we can give you fluids and medications more easily over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was a little nervous about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s perfectly safe. A chest X-ray confirmed it’s in the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your MRCP results back. It shows some mild changes in the pancreatic duct, which fits with your history of pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there a blockage or a pseudocyst?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, no blockages or pseudocysts. That’s good news. The changes are from past inflammation, not a new complication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the liver spots I’ve had before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still there—two small hemangiomas, unchanged. Nothing to worry about.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain today? Still needing the PCA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I’ve been using it less. Can I try some liquids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with clear liquids—water, broth, popsicles. We’ll go slow and see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m so ready to eat something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve kept down popsicles and broth. We’ll advance you to a soft diet today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. But I’ve been having more bowel movements lately. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were constipated before, so we started a bowel regimen. We checked for C. diff because of your history, and it was negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was worried it was an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s likely just the laxatives. We’ll adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is much better. We’re switching you from the PCA to oral hydromorphone as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I stop the IV fluids soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep the PICC for now. You might need it for nutrition if your intake stays low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning a change. Your right PICC had some issues, so we’re placing a new one on the left side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another procedure? Is it necessary?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to ensure reliable access. The old line wasn’t flowing well. The new one will help with fluids and possible nutrition support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your new PICC is in place and working well. We’ll start parenteral nutrition today to help you regain strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nutrition through the IV? Why not just eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your appetite is still low, and we want to make sure you’re getting enough calories and nutrients while your pancreas heals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. How long will I need that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A few days, maybe a week. We’ll reassess based on how well you eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re making great progress. Pain is well-controlled with oral meds, and you’re eating soft foods without issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If this continues, likely in the next two to three days. We’ll make sure you can manage pain at home and have a plan for follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning your discharge for tomorrow. We’ll send you home with hydromorphone for pain, phenergan to help with nausea, and reglan to help your stomach empty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I still need the PICC?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we’ll remove it before you leave. You’re eating well enough now that you don’t need IV nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about my depression meds? I’ve been on Wellbutrin and Zoloft.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re simplifying to bupropion and sertraline, which are the same as Wellbutrin and Zoloft. And trazodone at night as needed for sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night you tolerated a regular diet. That’s a big step. We’ll remove the PICC this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m really glad to hear that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: PICC is out, and you’re doing well. Discharge is set for tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I was really scared this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But you responded well to treatment. Just take it slow at home—advance your diet gradually, and use pain meds as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Here’s your discharge summary and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call your doctor if pain worsens or you can’t keep food down. And follow up with your gastroenterologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you for explaining everything along the way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and I hope you stay feeling better.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a history of recurrent pancreatitis was admitted due to a relapse of severe right epigastric pain shortly after discharge from a prior hospitalization. She was initially kept NPO and managed with IV fluids and a hydromorphone PCA for pain control. Imaging with MRCP showed chronic changes consistent with prior pancreatitis but no acute complications. A PICC line was placed for fluid and medication access, later replaced due to poor flow. Parenteral nutrition was initiated to support nutritional recovery. Her pain improved, allowing transition to oral medications and gradual advancement of diet. Diarrhea was attributed to a new bowel regimen, with negative C. difficile testing. She was discharged home in improved condition with a plan for oral pain management, GI follow-up, and continuation of psychiatric medications.
